#4665. Let’s Not Scroll to the Next Forever

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Chris Moody was a senior political correspondent with CNN for many years and is now a journalism professor at Appalachian State University in Boone, NC. He lives in a log cabin in a mountain hollow with his wife and their three-year-old son. The cabin has no cell signal. Over three years ago, they cancelled their home internet and went with a landline (intended to be a temporary measure for one summer). They write about it all in their Substack, The Opt Outers. I interviewed him about why willpower can’t compete with our devices, and what people who can’t move to the mountains can do instead.

Yael Hallak: I deleted my social media accounts six months ago. Then I came across the password to an old Instagram account, and I'm back to scrolling. I can't move to the mountains. What can we do as a species?

Chris Moody: The tech companies know what grabs our attention, and they feed it to us (that's how they make their money). Billions of dollars are being thrown at us, and no human will ever be able to win that battle every time, whether you're trying to find an old password or simply want to switch your mind off.

So create what I call a Sabbath space — a room, a floor, a corner of the house, where these technologies simply can't go in. Some people go down the route of "landlining," where the phone is left plugged in on the kitchen counter, and you're only allowed to use it there, standing. What would have been three hours on the couch comes down to three minutes. Think about whether you actually need Wi-Fi at all or whether a wired connection in one room would be sufficient. And make the rules when you're sober; you don't want to be relying on yourself when you're drunk.

CM: Even if you're not using it, the phone is still calling; it's like the sirens calling out to Odysseus. Every moment is a decision, and decision fatigue wins. That's why we have a scoop of ice cream at 9 p.m. and not at 9 a.m.

I drove fifteen minutes to a studio for this interview. My couch would have been far easier, but it's worth it. When I'm finished in town, the laptop goes down, and at home I couldn't have checked email if I'd wanted to. The people who need me have my landline. I'm not living in the 1890s, more in the 1990s.

YK: During the recent bank and flight outages, I was constantly refreshing X. Information is what makes me feel in control. My husband is always telling me to put the phone down and look out of the window.

CM: Today's channels don't give you any data that's going to help. They just feed an appetite that can't be quenched; they're just empty calories. You can learn what you need from the Sunday New York Times once a week. A reporter on a presidential campaign needs real time. Most people don't.

Look at the boomers, the richest generation in history, spending their days being angry online. Do they have more information? Possibly. Are they any happier? No.

YK: You teach undergrads; how are they getting on?

CM: They know the monster is coming for them and they think they've been had. Some of them, the ones brought up by phone-obsessed parents, are completely radicalised: "I'll never ignore my child the way my own did." When they see my Nokia flip phone, they go absolutely mental, and a few of them come back with "I've got one!" They're just as hooked as everyone else, just as keen to get their hands on one, but they're thinking about it very carefully. I'm hopeful.

YK: So many people want this life. What enabled you to get it?

CM: My first real job post-college was in social media (at the very beginning of it), and I saw what the algorithms did to my friends. I'm an extrovert, a golden retriever when the doorbell rings, and suddenly everyone just went off and into their screens. Mostly it's my wife, really. She's the one who drives it. Left to my own devices, I go with the flow.

YK: What do you do at dinners where everyone's on their phone?

CM: At our place, it just works itself out as we don't have phones. People come and ask for the Wi-Fi password, and I say we don't have one; there's a landline if you want it. They never do. We don't have to take the rubbish we've been given; we can just eat the better stuff.

YK: Is there anything you're missing? Podcasts, audiobooks?

CM: Not at all. I download the episodes in town and listen to them at home whilst doing the dishes. On Friday nights we watch a library DVD on a projector and a pull-down screen. It takes ten minutes to set it up, and that friction is important. Everything has a beginning and an end. It's not "let's just scroll to the next forever." It's: that's all we've got.

YK: So you just have more willpower than the rest of us?

CM: No! I have absolutely no willpower. I'm a disaster. When I'm on the road, and there's Wi-Fi all over the place, I just go absolutely mad and end up with no idea how the time has gotten away from me. The solution is systems, really. Less friction for the good things, more for the bad. In New York, we put our phones in baskets by the door, and we had the router on a timer, which would turn it off from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. If we're going to rely on willpower, we're all going to fail. We all are.

#4664. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4663. Genesis reveals GV90 prices start at $100K+ in Korea, but it will cost more for coach doors

Genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis said the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a new realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

The GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

To power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

And.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

#4662. I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

Plus, the expert-backed reason a few minutes of mobility can add up over time.

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” says Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”

And just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

My routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

Heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

By the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

However, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”

Kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

#4661. The Best Winter Jackets for Men, Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

We tried more than 40 options to find the ones worth wearing all season.

MEN’S HEALTH EDITORS spend a lot of time outdoors. We commute to our NYC office, then juggle the gym, errands, and weekend outings. So when cold weather hits, we need winter coats that can get us through nearly every icy scenario imaginable. Gone are the days when staying warm meant looking like a walking snowman. Today’s outerwear pairs advanced insulation with weather-resistant fabrics and thoughtful details to help keep you warm when the temperatures drop. The best designs layer comfortably, move well, and still look sharp.

As someone who tests gear year-round—and as part of a team that’s been reviewing winter coats since 2019—I’ve worn everything from lightweight puffers on frosty commutes to parkas in sub-zero conditions. Along the way, the Men’s Health style team has put more than 40 coats through real-life use: daily city commutes, snowy trail days, and ski trips. We look at how warm they actually feel, how well they move, how tough the materials are, and whether they look good off the rack. And after all that, Mack Weldon, Columbia, and Canada Goose rose to the top as the best winter coats for men.

I’ve been getting my wear out of Mack Weldon’s WarmKnit Air Hooded Jacket for the past year and it surprised me with its performance. At first glance, you’d think it’s just a lightweight puffer built for those mild 50- to 60-degree temps. But I found it could hang in the 40s, too—and still keep me warm. That’s thanks to its Thinsulate fill, synthetic insulation made of ultra-fine fibers, which does the heavy lifting without making me feel like a bloated marshmallow. It’s water- and wind-resistant, so a little drizzle or gusty wind doesn’t ruin a commute either.

The snap-button front and the two-way zipper make it easy to get in and out of, and the structured hood actually stays put, protecting your head without flopping around or blowing off. Just like most of Mack Weldon’s winter collection, sporty casual meets performance is the vibe here, so you can wear it with anything from a sweatsuit to a casual crewneck over chinos. With bonded quilting and interior pockets, it's both functional and polished, so it works for weekend hikes or casual dinners.

That said, there are trade‑offs. The jacket’s waist‑length cut means it won’t cover your core the way a mid‑thigh parka does, so in truly cold winter conditions you’ll feel more exposed around hips and lower back. If you need serious warmth for winter storms, opt for a longer cut; if you want a versatile everyday coat for mild to moderately cold weather, this is a standout value pick.

For days when you want warmth without the bulk, this Columbia down jacket delivers in spades. It uses Omni‑Heat reflective lining—those tiny silver dots that bounce your body heat back at you—which helps keep heat where you want it even as temperatures dip and winds pick up. It’s the kind of jacket you reach for when you want to feel cozy without feeling weighed down.

The 650‑fill down has enough loft to stay warm without ballooning your silhouette, and the baffle construction keeps insulation evenly distributed while creating a streamlined look that’s more polished than many puffers of similar warmth. Columbia also packs in tech‑forward features like HeatSeal construction to trap warmth while still allowing breathability and Omni‑Shield for moisture resistance and stain repellency—handy when you’re trudging through slush or, as I once did, surviving a spilled coffee on the way to the bus.

What I appreciate most is how easily it layers: It slips over a fleece or hoodie without feeling stiff, and it’s comfortable enough to wear all day whether you’re heading to work or exploring snowy trails. It’s not the warmest jacket around, but for everyday winter conditions where you want mobility and comfort with insulation, it’s a fantastic pick.

This is, quite simply, one of the best budget winter jackets we’ve tested—and it’s worth your attention even if you usually steer clear of ultra‑affordable picks. Deals and Trends Editor Tim Kohut wore the coat zipped up, and found that the heavyweight insulation did a solid job at keeping the shivers at bay on a brisk walk to the train — all without overheating once he hit the warm subway platform.

The polyester shell is water-repellent, not waterproof, so he can survive light showers without them soaking through to his clothes. It may not be the best option for heavy rain, so if you’re staring down a prolonged rainstorm, an umbrella or rain layer is still a smart call. Its relaxed fit is roomy enough for you to fit a chunky sweater underneath without bulk. Kohut rocked a T-shirt and chunky cardigan, and did not feel like the Michelin Man after being fully zipped up. The hood doesn’t cinch tight — one of the few real drawbacks — which lets cold air sneak in on windier days, but it is fleece‑lined for extra comfort and warmth.

Pockets are straightforward but functional, and the simple styling means this jacket works for daily commuting as easily as casual weekends. For the price, it’s a total win if you want something warm, reliable, and unfussy without dropping big cash.

Our Grooming Editor Sean Zucker wore this parka in every cold-weather situation: long commutes, chilly hikes, snowball fights. It has a slim puffer design but with a longer cut and more down, making it warmer for bone-chilling morning walks to the coffee shop. Zucker recently got caught in a sudden downpour, and the waterproof—not just water-resistant—shell kept him completely dry. On a freezing 30-degree cold and windy day, he stayed warm and comfortable the entire time. Plus, the storm cuffs blocked icy gusts from sneaking in at the sleeves.

He also appreciated the two-way zipper, which you don’t see on a lot of winter coats. It made hopping on and off the subway or sitting at a café easy without feeling restricted. While the insulated hood isn’t super spacious, it cinches close enough to trap heat. The fit is stylish without feeling bulky, and his hands fit perfectly in the pockets—small detail, but it really makes a difference when it’s freezing out. Yes, it’s an investment piece, but with premium 700-fill down warmth, waterproof and windproof protection, and thoughtful features, this parka is a true workhorse built to handle harsh conditions.

Canada Goose’s coat may come with some sticker shock, but our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan has made good use of it for the past three winters. He wears it to walk his two corgis, and between the snow, wind, and icy sidewalks, it keeps him warm without feeling like he’s lugging around a heavy sleeping bag. The Arctic Tech fabric—a polyester-cotton blend—has structure without stiffness, so it handles those brutal days when the wind tries to cut straight through you. Its longer silhouette offers extra coverage in snowy conditions. Not to mention, it’s a stylish coat, so you’re getting warmth and thoughtful design versus a bulky, shapeless puffer.

Like Fjallraven’s parka, this one has more pockets than your average coat—four outside, three inside. Two are great for thawing frozen mitts, and the others have flaps that help secure smaller essentials like a wallet, beanie, or winter gloves. There’s even a down-filled hood that feels toasty without making you feel stuffy, plus backpack-style straps if you want to carry it hands-free while running errands or grabbing coffee.

Sure, it’s very pricey, but we had to bite the bullet and think about the bigger picture. Stepping outside doesn’t feel like wrestling with the elements anymore. Between warmth, thoughtful design, and sleek style, it’s become our go-to armor for extreme weather—and it’s already survived three ruthless winter seasons in a row.

Men’s Health designer Jason Speakman took this burly parka from Fjallraven out on the slopes during a trip to Aspen. At 6 feet tall with a slender build, he found that this jacket wasn’t suffocating or too heavy, letting him flex, bend, and twist easily while carving turns or easing down steep trails. The fleece-lined hood with detachable faux fur edging kept his head and ears warm on icy chairlift rides, and he could easily remove the fur for a sleeker après-ski look. Thanks to the drawcords at the neck, it pulls tight around your face to shut out breezes.

This coat has eight pockets—more than any on the list—including roomy zippered chest pockets that fit slim essentials like a phone or cardholder. Its weight-to-warmth ratio is excellent; after five hours on the snow, Speakman stayed warm without feeling like he was wearing a stiff, overstuffed parka. The fit is generous, allowing space to pile base layers and still keep a clean profile.

Down and synthetic insulation are two of the most common options.

Synthetic insulation is made from polyester fibers, more affordable than down, and handles wet weather better. Popular options include PrimaLoft and Thinsulate, which use a blend of synthetic fibers designed to trap heat while remaining lightweight and breathable.

Down is made from clusters of goose or duck plumage, and is prized for its lightweight warmth. It compresses easily for packing and offers superior heat retention in dry conditions. Some coats even blend down and synthetic fill to combine the benefits of both.

Look for a waterproof shell, sealed seams, and a protective hood to help keep rain and snow from soaking through. Features like adjustable cuffs and storm flaps can also help block out wind and moisture. If you’re dealing with wet, snowy winters, prioritize a fully waterproof design over a water-resistant finish.

A winter coat should leave enough room to layer a sweater or hoodie without feeling bulky or restricting movement. The shoulders should sit comfortably, the sleeves should cover the wrists, and the hem should provide enough coverage for your needs. If you plan to wear it over heavier layers, consider sizing up, but always check the brand’s fit recommendations.

Look for fleece-lined hand pockets to keep your fingers warm and interior pockets to protect your phone, wallet, or AirPods from the cold. Extra details like zippered or hidden pockets add practicality, especially for commuting, travel, or outdoor adventures.

Our fashion team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, tested more than 40 winter coats in real-world conditions, from freezing city commutes to snowy hikes, ski trips, and travel days spent shuffling between cold-weather airports. If a coat claimed to handle winter, we made sure it proved it. We focused on warmth, durability, fit, mobility, and practicality. We paid attention to how each coat insulated in different temperatures, whether the materials could stand up to wind and wet weather, how well the coat moved with us during long days out, and whether the design felt useful rather than overbuilt.

Details like pocket placement, zippers, adjustability, and overall comfort played a big role too. After months of wear and side-by-side comparisons, only the top performers made our final list. These are the winter coats that stayed warm, held up, and made our lives easier—not just in theory, but in brutal winter reality.

For most of us, the terms "jacket" and "coat" are probably interchangeable. However, the main difference comes down to length and coverage. A winter coat's main objective is to keep you warm, which is why it's bigger and thicker, extends past the hips or toward the knees, and is filled with some type of insulation. A jacket, on the other hand, is considered a combination of style and warmth. Jackets don't typically go past the waist and they're designed to be worn indoors at times. Winter jackets can be layered more with outfits too—sometimes even under a coat.

Winter jackets can work as your main outer layer in cold weather, especially when they’re insulated and long enough to provide adequate coverage. For colder temperatures or extended time outdoors, a longer, more heavily insulated coat or parka can provide additional warmth and protection. The right choice ultimately depends on the weather, your activity level, and how much you plan to layer underneath.

#4660. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

#4659. When Life Becomes Frantic, We Slip into Autopilot

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

The world moves faster now than ever before. Rapidly accelerating technology and AI development build on each other exponentially, compressing the time it takes for major shifts to occur. Digital tools and instant communication are efficient but can also foment a work culture that embraces around-the-clock demands. Nonstop access to news, social media, and other content floods our brains with more input than we can process. This is all compounded by the overwhelming experience of poly-crisis, that is, multiple global challenges that are continuous, interconnected, and amplify one another as they collide. The bombardment of these factors can keep our brains in a low-grade fight-or-flight state.

When demands become constant, unrelenting, and urgent, your brain likely shifts from deliberate decision-making mode to automatic routines to save mental energy (Wirz, Bogdanov, and Schwabe, 2018). Research shows that approximately two-thirds of our daily actions are driven by habit rather than conscious decision-making (Rebar and colleagues, 2026). When your days fly by on autopilot, they become indistinguishable and leave you feeling spent, overwhelmed, and exhausted. Living a more intentional life and staying grounded in your body and the present moment means stepping away from autopilot and bringing conscious choice back to your days.

Learning to live with more intention starts by cultivating an awareness that your days have become blurred and indistinct, filled with routines and unexamined habits, and dominated by pressured reactions rather than intentional responses. Stop for a moment and ask: Where is all my urgent energy taking me? Is there a clear finish line? Do I just push through, day after day?

Becoming more intentional means knowing the direction you are aiming for, with the sense that your goals are worth pursuing. A strong sense of purpose has been linked to better physical health and emotional well-being, including better sleep, lower cortisol/stress, greater mental clarity, a stronger immune system, and enhanced resilience (Kim and colleagues, 2022).

Intention means taking the time to notice a moment with your full attention. When your mind is busy replaying events from the past or is perseverating on what might happen in the future, you are no longer present. You become disconnected and are likely stuck on high alert. When this happens, your brain’s ability to encode new information becomes impaired, making it harder to take in what is happening around you. Living with intention means paying attention and staying present in the moment, with mindfulness and without judgment. You can practice this with simple behaviors aimed at increasing brief moments of noticing. For example, pause for a few deep breaths before entering a meeting and ask yourself what matters most as you arrive. You can simplify this further. Whenever you switch tasks or enter a new setting, take a deep, mindful breath and say to yourself, “Arriving.”

Another way to enhance your awareness is to turn routine tasks, such as washing the dishes or taking a shower, into anchors for staying present. We tend to rush through these without really taking notice. These tasks offer perfect opportunities to slow down and notice what the water feels like and listen to the sounds around you. Adding a moment of gratitude, where you acknowledge small joys or blessings, helps shift your perspective from what is missing to what you have in the moment.

You do not need to retool your entire schedule to feel present. Small, low-effort shifts can interrupt automatic habits. Any little thing that introduces novelty can move your brain from automatic processing into active awareness—use your non-dominant hand while brushing your teeth or take an unfamiliar route home. When your brain encounters something unexpected, your internal predictions fail, and you are rewarded with a dopamine surge as your focus sharpens and awareness is enhanced as your brain moves out of autopilot.

Setting clear boundaries with yourself is something else to consider. Rather than a cluttered mind and desk, intention means actively choosing where your energy goes. Multi-tasking can take you away from intentionality. Instead, train yourself to be present with each activity. When you are eating, just eat. If you are driving, just focus on the drive. Your decisions, big and small, can be honed to better reflect your genuine priorities, such as health or creativity.

Finally, think about how you respond to messages and questions throughout your day. Rather than urgently reacting to each communication, you might pause for a reflective breath before responding. Slow down so that your nervous system remains balanced and calm. If you notice tension building or you rush through messages, step away for a brief time-out to bring yourself back into the present. Ask yourself whether the speed is actually necessary or just an ingrained habit.

Living with intention is not a single decision. It is an ongoing practice. At the end of the day, take a moment to look back and ask, “Where did my time go? What reflected my values? What did not?” These small practices add up so that the gap between the life you are living and the life you intend to live begins to narrow.

Kim, E. S., Chen, Y., Nakamura, J. S., Ryff, C. D., & VanderWeele, T. J. (2022). Sense of Purpose in Life and Subsequent Physical, Behavioral, and Psychosocial Health: An Outcome-Wide Approach. American journal of health promotion: AJHP, 36(1), 137–147. https://doi.org/10.1177/08901171211038545

Rebar, A. L., Vincent, G., Kovac Le Cornu, K., & Gardner, B. (2026). How habitual is everyday life? An ecological momentary assessment study. Psychology & Health, 41(9), 1507–1532. https://doi.org/10.1080/08870446.2025.2561149

Wirz, L., Bogdanov, M., & Schwabe, L. (2018). Habits under stress: Mechanistic insights across different types of learning. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences, 20, 9–16. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cobeha.2017.08.009

#4658. Get the Women’s Health Beginner Workout Plan: 4-Week Strength Training and Cardio Program

It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately. My feed is full of people hitting the weights for the first time ever or setting big goals like getting their first pull-up. And let me just say: It’s awesome!

So, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party. When you’re starting to work out, it can be hard to sift through all the options and find a program that’s actually accessible for a true beginner (or, someone restarting after quite some time). That is, until now.

The Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey. This comprehensive program guides you through strength and cardio workouts that only take between 20 and 45 minutes. And, of course, it answers every burning question you could have about starting a fitness routine.

No matter your age or experience, starting an exercise routine has many benefits, says Kristen McParland, CPT, your coach for the next four weeks. Building muscle increases total-body strength; your bones, ligaments, and tendons get healthier; and even your blood pressure and immunity may improve. So lace up those sneakers and we’ll see you at the gym now, too.

Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan

Over the next four weeks, you’ll follow a specific plan each day, focusing either on strength training, optional cardio, active recovery, or rest (more on these, below). Each strength workout includes a warm-up and a cooldown (which you can use on cardio days, too). More info on each below.

Simply follow the instructions of each full-body strength training workout in the Women's Health+ Beginner Workout Plan. You can find detailed how-to instructions for each exercise in the Exercise Guide section of the PDF.

Equipment Needed: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a step or box, and a slam ball. Don’t have access to a kettlebell or slam ball? Don't worry—you can still do those exercises with a dumbbell.

Cardio is important for everyone, regardless of fitness level or routine. That’s because when you’re lifting heavy, your heart needs to be able to take on that stress. Training cardio—through running, cycling, or brisk walking—will help improve your heart strength.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Complete 20 to 30 minutes of running, biking, cycling, rowing, or using the elliptical or stair climber (whatever you enjoy). No matter which form of cardio you choose, start with interval training: exert yourself for 30 seconds, then go at a light pace for 1 to 2 minutes, alternating the pattern for a total of 20 minutes. The goal is to “get your heart rate up, but then pull it back and recover,” McParland says. Eventually, you’ll be able to decrease the rest time and maintain that higher-intensity movement for 15 to 20 minutes without a break.

Your activity on this day is up to you. The goal is to do some kind of low-intensity movement lasting 20 minutes. Some ideas: outdoor walk or hike, bike ride, incline treadmill walk, yoga, or Pilates class.

Take this day to relax so your muscles have time to repair. Still, if your body is craving some type of activity for recovery, you could stretch, go for a walk, or even try a treatment like a massage, sauna, or cold-plunge session.

Here’s how things will progress each week.

Complete the five programmed workouts when it’s convenient for you. Focus on your form and take your two rest days when you need to recover.

If you completed all the workouts in Week 1, repeat them during Week 2, adjusting one variable in your routine, McParland says: the number of reps or sets, the weight, the speed of the moves (slower is harder). If you missed a workout, don’t stress. Refocus on completing all of the Week 1 workouts before making any of the changes above.

You’ve officially done two full weeks of this workout plan—nice job! During this third week, repeat the workouts from Week 2 in exactly the same way or adjust one variable again (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, and rest periods). If you feel you’re crushing it and are ready to level up, try the third full-body strength workout.

Still going strong? Thought so! Hit all six workouts and adjust one variable per workout for an extra challenge (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, rest time). You can also ramp up your cardio time (to 30 to 40 minutes) or speed, shorten rest intervals (for interval training), or raise your step goal by 10 percent (e.g., if your daily step goal was 5,000 a day, make it 5,500).

Ready to become your strongest self? Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan now.

When you’re just beginning to work out, do a minimum of two full-body strength training days each week, McParland recommends. During both of those days, you should hit at least one exercise from each category of the foundational movement patterns. This will give you enough of a challenge to stimulate muscle growth, she says.

During the first two weeks of this plan, you will have two strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will 20 to 30 minutes), one day of active rest (a stint of low-intensity movement lasting at least 20 minutes), and two recovery days, for a total of five workouts per week.

After those two weeks, see how your body feels and if your body is craving a third day of full-body training. If so, progress to the next phase of this plan. That weekly schedule consists of three strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will run 20 to 30 minutes), one active rest day (lasting at least 20 minutes), and one recovery day, for a total of six workouts per week. If your body isn’t ready for three strength-training days yet, wait another two weeks. Once you’ve completed the full four weeks of this plan, consider adding in the third day.

Start with medium weights that will challenge you for 10 to 12 reps, says Sariya. Essentially, you’ll want to feel you’ve reached 70 to 80 percent of your rate of perceived exertion (i.e., your fatigue level is at a 7 or 8 out of 10) by the time you’re doing your final reps in a set. When you feel you can do more than 12 reps, it’s time to increase your weight, but keep the same number of reps. This way, you’re always working toward your goal of building strength.

As for how much to increase by: a good rule of thumb is 2.5 to 5 pounds for an upper-body exercise and 5 to 10 pounds for a lower-body move.

What if I need to rest in the middle of a set?

Resting during a workout is important—if you don’t take enough time to recover between exercises, you won’t have enough energy in your body for the next one. With this plan, you’ll rest between moves in a superset or tri-set for 20 to 30 seconds, or however long it takes to transition between exercises. Between supersets and tri-sets, you’ll rest for one minute.

If you get fatigued in the middle of a set, push through if you feel safe doing so, Sariya says. However, if you feel dizzy or fear you might drop a weight on yourself, put it down and take time to recover. When you’re feeling better, you can start again. If you’re in any sort of pain, stop the workout entirely.

Cardio is a great supplement to strength training, McParland says. Plus, it has a slew of benefits, such as better endurance in strength training, better blood pressure regulation, and higher VO2 max, she says.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Pick any form of cardio you enjoy, whether that’s brisk walking, running, cycling, or swimming, and sprinkle it in two or three days a week for 20 to 30 minutes, McParland recommends.

On an active rest day, you’ll still exercise a bit through low-intensity movement, like a leisurely bike ride or hike. On a recovery day, you’ll do just that: recover. After all, you need to give your muscles time to rebuild and repair, Sariya says. But to maximize the recovery aspect, you can also opt to stretch, go for a gentle walk, or even get a self-care body treatment like a massage.

Once you’ve got the WH+ Beginner Workout Plan under your belt, you’re ready to take things to another level. One way to do that is by simply restarting the program—and completing the moves with heavier weights this time. (This is called progressive overload, and it’s another foundational concept in strength training. The idea is that over time, you will keep increasing the stimulus to your muscles to continuously challenge them and make them stronger.)

Picking the right weight is an art as much as it is a science, but for a general rule of thumb, for upper-body moves, increase your weights by 2.5 to 5 pounds and see how that feels. For lower-body ones, try adding 5 to 10. You should feel like you’re ending each set two to three reps away from failure (where your form starts to break down). You can tell you’re close if your range of motion starts to shorten or your reps are slowing down. That’s how you know you’re successfully challenging yourself. And, if you don’t happen to have a lot of different-sized weights at your disposal, you can always just increase the number of reps you do instead.

But, if you’re looking for something new, WH+ has a bunch of other trainer-created programs to help you grow your knowledge and confidence in the gym and attack other fitness goals.

High cheekbones and a narrow forehead and chin look great with rimless or oval frames of sunglasses because they emphasize your eyes and soften your facial angles.

When choosing a new pair of sunglasses, you should make sure that they provide 100 percent UV protection against both UVA and UVB rays. Otherwise, you can find yourself in a world of problems. As for what type to consider, go with wraparound models as they block UV rays that come in from the side and shield against winds that can cause dry eyes.

Polarized lenses are designed to cut down harsh glare, which helps reduce eye strain and makes it easier to see clearly in bright conditions. That glare usually comes from light bouncing off flat surfaces like water, snow, or pavement, not just direct sunlight. Polarized technology works by filtering out light, so you’re not squinting or dealing with that blinding shine. Because of that, polarized sunglasses are especially useful for water sports and outdoor activities, while photochromic lenses (which adjust to changing light) are recommended for everyday use.

Finding the right pair of sunglasses has everything to do with a frame that works for your face, style, and how you live in them. #4656. Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg.

Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”

Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”

That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

That’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

#4655. You'll Change Your Mind: The Messages Asexual Women Remember

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Have you ever been told something that stuck with you long after the conversation ended?

Maybe it was a piece of advice from a parent, like "money doesn't grow on trees," or encouragement from a teacher who believed in you when you didn't believe in yourself.

As communication researchers, we call these memorable messages—statements that stay with us over time, shaping how we understand ourselves, our relationships, and the world around us. Some offer reassurance or guidance. Others communicate expectations about who we should be or how our lives should unfold.

Asexuality is commonly defined as experiencing little to no sexual attraction, although it exists on a spectrum. Asexual individuals may experience romantic attraction, pursue relationships, marry, or have children. Their sexual orientation does not necessarily determine their interest in relationships, sexual activity, or parenthood.

Despite this diversity, asexuality remains widely misunderstood and is often characterized as an invisible sexuality. Asexual individuals frequently encounter assumptions that their identity is temporary, invalid, or something that needs to be fixed.

For asexual women, these misconceptions intersect with societal expectations surrounding relationships, marriage, and motherhood. When these milestones are treated as universal expectations, women whose identities or choices differ may find themselves having to explain or defend them.

To better understand these experiences, we asked asexual women across the United States to recall memorable messages they had received about childbearing. Of the 126 individuals who participated in our study, 107 recalled a memorable message—and 94% were negative.

Five themes emerged from their responses:

1. Motherhood as an obligation. Some women recalled messages framing motherhood as a biological, religious, or social responsibility rather than a personal choice.

One woman recalled being told by a male friend that she was "selfish " for 'choosing' to be asexual and not having children and... wasn't really a woman."

2. Family expectations and interpersonal pressure. Other messages emphasized the desires of parents and grandparents, particularly their expectations of having grandchildren.

Another woman recalled, "My mother insisted that she was suffering because I was depriving her of grandchildren."

3. Fear of a life without children. Participants also received warnings suggesting that choosing not to have children would inevitably lead to loneliness or regret.

One woman remembered being told, "[I]f you don't have children you'll end up forgotten as an elderly person and die alone."

4. Identity invalidation through future predictions. Some of the most familiar messages suggested that participants' identities or reproductive preferences were temporary. As one participant explained, "I remember hearing what most people used to say: 'It's a phase', 'You'll change your mind one day', 'I used to think I didn't want kids either until I met your father/mother.' Because what if I don't? What if I really don't want children?"

Rather than accepting women's understanding of their own identities and aspirations, these messages assumed their futures would eventually align with conventional expectations.

5. Social scrutiny and judgment. Participants described having their sexuality and reproductive choices questioned or dismissed. One participant recalled being told, "[A] woman can't be asexual and want kids. That is senseless...just say you're a lesbian."

These messages share a common assumption: There is a particular way women are supposed to experience sexuality, relationships, and motherhood.

One of the most striking findings from our study was what participants were told, but by whom. Nearly 70% of the memorable messages were communicated by other women (e.g., mothers, other family members, and friends). This raises an interesting question: Why do women sometimes reinforce the same expectations that have historically limited their own choices?

Gender norms are learned, communicated, and reproduced through everyday interactions, including conversations between mothers and daughters, among friends, and across generations.

Women who have been taught that motherhood is central to a fulfilling life may communicate that belief to others, sometimes without recognizing the pressure it creates.

For instance, one participant recalled, "My mom and grandma talk about it every time I see them because I'm getting older. They make fun of me for not having kids yet and me ending our bloodline."

In this example, motherhood becomes more than an individual decision. It becomes a family expectation, one tied to ideas about lineage, responsibility, and what women owe to previous generations. Of course, we cannot know whether the women sending these messages intend to cause harm. A mother expressing concern about her daughter's future may genuinely believe she is offering helpful advice. But intentions and impacts are not always the same. These interactions illustrate how cultural expectations can be passed down through relationships, even by people who have experienced those same pressures themselves.

The consequences of these memorable messages extended beyond the original conversations. Some participants described feeling ashamed, misunderstood, or uncertain about their identities. Others reported becoming more confident in their decisions, even when the messages themselves were hurtful.

One participant described how her mother's repeated comments about motherhood affected their relationship: "It has negatively affected my relationship with my mother even though she does not realize it. I am content with being asexual and my stance on being childfree."

Some participants became more outspoken about their boundaries. One woman recalled being told that her asexuality must have resulted from trauma and that therapy could "fix" her. Rather than reconsidering her identity, she explained, "It's made me more proactive about telling people children are entirely off the table for me. I don't allow others to even entertain the thought that they can convince me or somehow change my mind."

Although our research focused on asexual women, the findings invite us to reconsider how we talk about other people's futures. How often do we ask about marriage, relationships, or children without considering whether those are milestones someone actually wants? And how frequently do we respond to someone's choices by insisting they'll eventually change their mind?

Of course, asking about someone's future is not inherently harmful. These conversations can be meaningful ways of connecting with people we care about. But there is a difference between expressing curiosity about someone's life and communicating that their life should follow a particular path.

The messages we communicate can stay with people for years. Perhaps the most meaningful ones are those that make people feel understood rather than expected to become someone else.

Heuton, A. E., & Edwards, A. L. (2026). “You’ll change your mind”: A mixed-methods study of asexual women’s memorable messages about childbearing. LGBTQ+ Family: An Interdisciplinary Journal. doi.org/10.1080/27703371.2026.2748623

Cooke-Jackson, A., Gunning, J. N., & Rubinsky, V. (2025). Theory of memorable messages. Journal of Communication, 75(4), 259–272. doi.org/10.1093/joc/jqaf016

Denes, A., Clark, A. N., & Gunning, J. N. (2025). Memorable messages of asexuality. LGBTQ+ Family: An Interdisciplinary Journal. doi.org/10.1080/27703371.2025.2504912
