#4640. BYD’s full-size luxury SUV has a wheel problem, and it’s fixing it for free

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

After opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD said the issue stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The company said it “immediately” launched an investigation and corrected the issue so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit issues like this going forward.

BYD said the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

The company said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

#4639. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4638. Why We Get People Wrong

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

We get a lot of things wrong about one another. We often think we understand what other people think of us, and assume that the handful of actions we observe tells us something meaningful about their personality as a whole. Someone behaves rudely, and we conclude they are an unpleasant person. Someone struggles to find work, and we wonder whether they are trying hard enough. We interpret other people’s behaviour through our own experiences, expectations and beliefs, often with considerable confidence and remarkably little information1.

Psychologists have spent decades documenting the many ways our perceptions of others can be distorted; we are frequently wrong about others and even ourselves. These biases have consequences far beyond our interpersonal relationships. They shape whom we trust, whom we blame, what we believe people deserve and, ultimately, the institutions and policies we create and sustain.

Many of us feel we are living through unprecedented times. Particularly since 2020, rapid technological change, political polarisation and growing uncertainty about the future have made the world feel increasingly difficult to understand. But people have felt similarly at other points in history, and often with good reason.

In nineteenth-century Britain, the Industrial Revolution was transforming almost every aspect of society. Population growth, industrialisation and urbanisation brought extraordinary economic opportunities alongside increasingly visible poverty, overcrowding and disease. Governments were faced with social problems on a scale that existing institutions were poorly equipped to manage.

One response was the Poor Law Amendment Act of 18342.

For centuries, responsibility for assisting people experiencing poverty had rested largely with local parishes. Someone who became ill, lost their employment or could no longer support their family might receive money, food or other assistance without having to leave their home. The system was inconsistent, often ungenerous and increasingly expensive, but it afforded local authorities some discretion to respond to individual circumstances.

The 1834 reforms sought to make poor relief more efficient, less costly and less attractive to those thought capable of supporting themselves. Administration was reorganised, and assistance was increasingly tied to entering a workhouse. Relief outside the workhouse continued in some circumstances, for the sick and elderly, but even then, many elderly and disabled people still ended up in the workhouse.

Workhouses were deliberately designed to be places people would enter only out of desperation2. We are familiar with these institutions through Charles Dickens, whose Oliver Twist depicts a world in which poverty is often treated as a moral offence. Families were often separated, food really was gruel, and residents were subjected to arduous work and strict discipline. The severity was not an unfortunate consequence of inadequate resources but part of the intended deterrent.

The reasoning was straightforward enough: If assistance was too easy or readily available, people might become dependent upon it rather than seek employment. In fact, educating children was, in theory, supposed to be part of a workhouse remit, but in practice the standard varied considerably. Make assistance sufficiently unpleasant, and those capable of supporting themselves would presumably find a way to do so.

Of course, this reasoning depended on a particular understanding of why people were poor in the first place. A person unable to find employment, earning wages insufficient to support a family, or living with illness could not necessarily improve their circumstances through the threat of punishment. But policies built around assumptions about individual motivation often failed to account for precisely those conditions.

I don’t think the nineteenth-century reformers were simply cruel or stupid. They were attempting to manage substantial social and economic changes with the knowledge, institutions and political priorities available to them. Some were undoubtedly concerned with improving administration and reducing costs, while others had a more punitive understanding of poverty. The reforms also served the interests of those who wanted to reduce their contributions towards poor relief.

But the consequences illustrate something important: Our explanations of human behaviour influence the solutions we consider reasonable, even when those explanations are incomplete or mistaken.

Nearly two centuries later, we are living through another period of extraordinary transformation. Technology has changed how we work, communicate, form relationships and participate in society. Our scientific understanding of the world has expanded beyond anything nineteenth-century reformers could have imagined.

And, unlike our predecessors, we now possess the knowledge and technological capabilities to address many problems that once seemed insurmountable.

We have developed effective technologies that can substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions3. Advances in agriculture have enabled us to produce enough food globally to feed the world’s population, despite its extraordinary growth4. Vaccines, public health measures and medical research have given us tools to prevent and respond to devastating diseases.

But climate change continues, millions experience hunger, and preventable diseases still cause enormous suffering.

These problems are complex, and scientific and technological limitations remain. But increasingly, the question is not simply whether humanity possesses the knowledge or resources to improve people’s lives. The obstacles are frequently social, cultural, economic and political. They involve how resources are distributed, how institutions operate, whose interests they serve, and whether people can cooperate towards shared goals.

And underlying many of these obstacles are the explanations we give for why people believe and behave as they do.

Consider a more recent example of advocacy for punitive measures. Over several decades, psychiatrist James Gilligan studied violence in American prisons and sought to reform the way prisoners were treated5,6. In Massachusetts prisons, where violence, humiliation and abuse were commonplace, he developed reforms that emphasised treating prisoners with respect, providing psychological treatment and creating opportunities for education7.

Gilligan reported significant reductions in violence, and his research into prison education found extraordinarily low rates of reoffending among prisoners who completed college degrees. Even those regarded as among the most violent could, under different conditions, behave quite differently. But when William Weld became governor of Massachusetts in 1991, he opposed providing prisoners with free college education, arguing that people who couldn't afford university might start committing crimes just to get a degree in prison. His administration subsequently withdrew much of the state funding and undermined education delivery, despite reported drops in recidivism7,8. Sound familiar?

Neither understanding nor policy exists independently of the other. Our beliefs influence the systems we support, while those systems shape the circumstances and behaviours we subsequently observe. The resulting outcomes can then appear to confirm the assumptions that helped produce them—making the system self-reinforcing.

Institutions are also shaped by competing interests, and some people benefit considerably from arrangements that disadvantage others. Those with influence may understand perfectly well what a particular policy or economic incentive is likely to produce.

But the interests of a relatively small number of powerful actors can become difficult to challenge when much larger populations are persuaded that the existing arrangements serve their interests too, or that the problems those arrangements create are simply the fault of the individuals experiencing them.

This is where our understanding of one another becomes immensely consequential.

The way we explain another person’s circumstances influences how willing we are to help them, what we consider fair, and whether we recognise a problem as something that requires societal intervention. These explanations become part of our cultural understanding of how the world works, and help determine which institutions we defend and which we are prepared to change.

This blog is about those explanations: How we come to understand other people’s behaviour, why we so often get it wrong, and what the consequences are for the societies we live in. I’ll draw on research across psychology, biology, anthropology, and the social sciences to explore how individual behaviour interacts with the environments in which it develops. Sometimes that will mean examining the assumptions we make about our friends, strangers and, most importantly, ourselves. At other times, it will mean considering how those same assumptions influence our attitudes towards responsibility, inequality, politics and the institutions that govern our lives.

Understanding these processes is only part of the task. If we want different outcomes, we also have to use that understanding to change the conditions that produce them.

The nineteenth-century workhouse offers one illustration of what can happen when our assumptions about human behaviour inform our attempts to solve social problems. Seeing the same way of thinking manifest centuries later, despite all our accumulated knowledge, tells us something important about the real barriers to solving our problems.

One of the great challenges of our time is learning how to use knowledge to build societies that work better for the people living within them.

Perhaps a useful place to begin is by examining how much we still get wrong about one another and ourselves.

#4637. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4635. Should I Let My Child Play Grand Theft Auto?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Tomorrow, the biggest video game of all time will be released. The latest game in the blockbuster Grand Theft Auto series took 13 years and over a billion dollars to make. It’s predicted to be the biggest opening of any entertainment product in history.

The Grand Theft Auto games are an extremely violent, darkly satirical exploration of American culture. Currently, the game will only include a single-player story, but a multiplayer version is slated for release next year. I wrote previously about how to keep your kids safe while playing multiplayer games here.

It is unclear what content this game will include, as no one has discussed it publicly. If leaks are to be believed, the game will feature full nudity, including visible genitals and sex scenes. Based on previous entries, it will certainly feature drug use, offensive language including racial slurs, and frequent gun violence, including the ability to shoot police officers.

The game will absolutely not be meant for children. It is rated “M for Mature,” which means it is designed to be played only by people age 17 and older. However, many young people, especially high school boys, want to play it. I have worked with a number of young people who regularly play the previous game in the series, some of whom started as young as nine years old.

Some parents might decide to make an exception for their children, as they do with some R-rated movies. My parents let me watch some R-rated action movies like The Matrix as a young teenager, but they definitely would not have let me watch movies with explicit sexual content or graphic violence.

Parents understandably have questions about whether the game is appropriate and whether it will influence their children like the media suggests.

GTA games are extremely violent. I likely killed thousands of computer-controlled characters in the process of completing GTA V. They are not meant for children.

However, there is no evidence that the game, or any other violent media, will make players violent in the real world. The studies that purport to show a connection between violent video games and aggression often have serious methodological problems. Further, despite what the news media suggests, school shooters are actually less likely to enjoy violent video games than their peers. I wrote about this in more depth in a previous article.

Although video games are unlikely to make children violent, there is some evidence that our opinions and values can be shaped by the media we consume.

For example, people who live in the Nadroga province of Fiji had traditionally viewed larger bodies as healthy and desirable. This began to change starting in 1995 when they started receiving outside television signals. Researchers surveyed a group of teen girls within a month of American television reaching their region and again three years later. Historically, dieting was rare in this area, and none of the girls reported vomiting to control their weight in 1995. But by the second survey, 69 percent of these same girls had started to diet, and 11 percent had begun intentionally vomiting to control their weight. That is, just three years of exposure to Western media seems to have fundamentally altered how the entire region viewed body image.

Importantly, GTA is not alone in featuring problematic elements. Each can be found in other movies, games, and even the news on TV. It is unlikely that this game will be the first time an older teenager hears racial slurs or sexual language, or sees nudity or violence. Most recent R-rated crime movies feature all of the above. Modern horror movies like Saw or Hereditary feature much more graphic violence than GTA does. Ultimately, this is why the series’ satire is relevant; the games are simply a more extreme version of the culture in which many of us have grown up.

It is therefore unlikely that simply playing this game will have more of an effect on its players’ values than their other daily cultural experiences. The aforementioned girls in Fiji, whose body image was drastically changed, were being exposed to a foreign culture they had not experienced before. American teens are already saturated with media showing extreme violence, sexuality, and crime.

However, people who consume more violent media tend to believe that the world is more dangerous than it really is. Researchers who have studied this “mean world syndrome” have found that people who consume more media are more likely to fear violence and trust others less. If playing this game drastically increases the amount of time an individual spends consuming media, it is possible that they will believe themselves to be in more danger in the real world than they did before playing.

Parents who do not want their children to play this game should know that their children can simply download the game independently. Nearly all game consoles and computers now permit users to purchase the game digitally with a credit card or console-specific currency. To prevent this, concerned parents can set parental locks on game devices, including preventing purchases of games rated “M for Mature” (similar to blocking all R or NC-17 movies), or requiring a password before any digital purchases.

I also recommend that parents who are unsure whether their children should play such a game supervise their children or play along with them. As I wrote previously, this not only provides the opportunity to bond with children through their interests, but also lets parents talk about the game’s content and provide valuable context to what the children are experiencing. When the multiplayer version is eventually released, make sure that your kids are not chatting with strangers by turning off public chat.

Whether to let your children play a game like this is a personal decision. Reasonable parents can choose to ignore the recommended age if they understand the content of the game and believe their children are emotionally mature enough to consume it.

Below is a non-exhaustive list of questions parents should consider before purchasing the game for their children:

Grand Theft Auto VI will have a number of elements which most parents would find extremely objectionable. These are not likely to psychologically harm people who are mature enough to manage the subject matter and understand it in context.

However, the game’s content is highly inappropriate for most young people, and parents should proceed cautiously. If parents decide to buy it for their children, I recommend supervising them while playing and having open conversations about what their children are witnessing and experiencing.

Andrew is the author of Parenting a Gamer: Help Your Child Build Healthy Habits, Make Positive Choices, and Find Balance in Virtual Worlds.

#4634. Kia just made history at Germany’s most prestigious auto awards

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the new Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

#4633. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4632. Should Parents Genetically Enhance Their Children?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Imagine a world where everyone is healthy, intelligent, long-living, and happy. Intuitively, this seems wonderful, albeit unrealistic. However, recent scientific developments in genetic engineering, namely CRISPR-Cas, bring the question into public discourse: how the genetic enhancement of humans should be evaluated morally. This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

In 2001, when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) enabled parents to select from multiple embryos, Julian Savulescu introduced the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB), arguing that parents have obligations to choose the child expected to have the best life. In this post, I argue that accepting the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP) that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par commits one to accepting the parental obligation to genetically enhance their prospective children—that is, embryos—a position Savulescu doesn’t explicitly endorse but I argue is committed to.

Savulescu, Sandberg, and Kahane jointly propose the following definition for human enhancement: “[a]ny change in the biology or psychology of a person which increases the chances of leading a good life in the relevant set of circumstances.” According to this welfarist definition, a conception of normality is not needed to define enhancement, as we do not define an enhancement as being better than normal, but simply being better full stop. Medical treatments are therefore just a form of enhancement. If a genetic alteration in an embryo is not expected to lead to a better life for that human, then it is simply not an enhancement.

Consequentialists are only concerned with outcomes; how these outcomes are achieved is morally irrelevant. Killing and letting die are thus ceteris paribus morally equivalent. To formulate my argument:

(1) Those who want to be parents have the obligation to select the child that is expected to have the best life, or at least as good a life as the others, based on the relevant available information (= the PPB).

(2) Application of the PPB leads to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without the application of the PPB, based on the relevant available information.

(3) If act A and act B have the same expected consequences, then they are morally on par. (= the CP)

(4) Genetic enhancements in embryos lead to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without genetic enhancements, based on the relevant available information.

(5) Therefore, those who want to be parents have the obligation to genetically enhance embryos.

An objection often put forward is that genetic enhancements have risks that are too high or unknown and would make the life of the person targeted worse. However, when genetic alterations are expected to be more harmful than beneficial, they do not count as genetic enhancements and are therefore ruled out. Demanding a risk of zero to the targeted agents is over-demanding; otherwise, medical treatments would never be at the point they are today. In 2015, Chinese researchers released an article showing that the gene editing of human embryos is technologically possible.

Still, many therapies and treatments in medicine are often deemed obligatory, even though there is no consent, for example, vaccination. Also, everyone should be familiar with parents sending their children to school, even though their children might not have given their consent. As a child, I certainly wondered who gave my parents my permission to do so. Just as education makes us more autonomous, genetically increased intelligence would serve the same purpose. Genetic enhancements aim to increase rather than limit one's possible choices in life.

There is a rather famous critic against genetic enhancements from Mehlman and Botkin, that is, being too expensive and therefore even when all parents follow their obligation, the children of rich parents will be far more enhanced or those of poor parents won’t get any enhancements at all. Concerning the worry of unequal access through wealth, Savulescu argues that this is not an objection to the PPB, hence genetic enhancements, but to all purchases of benefits like better education or healthcare. If equality matters, then these benefits should be available to all.

That is to say, those who accept the PPB and the CP must bite the bullet and accept that parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. As a consequentialist, Julian Savulescu should have no problem doing so.

If you enjoyed this short essay, you might enjoy the much longer version, on which it is based, where I go into much more detail: click here.

Veit, W. (2018). Procreative beneficence and genetic enhancement. KRITERION – Journal of Philosophy, 32(1), 75–92. https://doi.org/10.1515/krt-2018-320105 [Download]

#4631. Albatross couple George and Geraldine reunite for the 10th straight year

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

The Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii has welcomed a special couple: George and Geraldine, two short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus). The birds have officially found each other for nesting season on the Midway Atoll for the 10th straight year in a row.  George was first spotted on October 18, and the pair was reunited by October 22.

Every fall, the remote group of islands becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, including the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any current bird species. One Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis), on the other hand, claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird—the famous Wisdom, who is over 70 years old.

Short-tailed albatrosses (called makalena in Hawaiian) are almost completely white and feature a large pink bill. They can live up to 50 years, and as exemplified by George and Geraldine, are monogamous. They nest on islands and atolls, and the species is listed as endangered by both the United States government and the state of Hawaii. At the turn of the 20th century, feather hunting almost made the species go extinct.

“The vast majority of breeding for short-tailed albatross occurs on remote islands in the western Pacific, including Torishima Island, Japan, which is an active volcano south of Tokyo, and the Senkaku Islands near Taiwan,” according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). “Since 2000, biologists at the [Midway Atoll National Wildlife] refuge have used short-tailed albatross decoys and audio playback of the seabird’s calls to attract more of them.”

In fact, George and Geraldine are the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, though other members of their species were spotted last season. They were banded as chicks on Torishima Island and first seen together on Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge in 2016. The cute pair brought their first chick into the world during the 2018-2019 breeding season.

“Millions of makalena once used their long wingspans to expertly glide on air currents across the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan to Alaska and Hawaiʻi,” the FWS writes. “The slowly growing population is estimated at around 10,000 today.”

BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology.

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

The setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.

Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.

Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

#4629. Voyager 1 is almost one light-day away from Earth

Published Nov 9, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Voyager 1, the NASA space probe that has traveled farther from Earth than any other human-made object, is closing in on a remarkable milestone. Actually, let’s call it a 16.09-billion-milestone. That’s the distance a photon can travel in a single day, which is to say the Voyager 1 spacecraft will be exactly one light-day away from our planet on November 18 at 5:18 a.m. EST.

At that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and then it would take another 24 hours for the probe’s response to come back. Imagine on a Friday morning telling your oven to turn on, but you don’t receive confirmation that it’s hot until Sunday. And by that point, the oven would have been baking whatever was inside for most of Saturday. That is the kind of delay that NASA’s Voyager team must work with.

Communicating with a machine at this superlative distance is “a pretty incredible endeavor,” Princeton University research scientist and heliophysicist Jamie S. Rankin tells Popular Science. Rankin is also a deputy project scientist of the Voyager mission. “In my mind the fun is receiving a signal back from the Voyager, a light-day away.”

Rankin and other astronomers use those signals to study the very local interstellar medium, which is the suburb of space surrounding our solar system. Voyager 1 has been in this region, about 11 billion miles away, since 2012. There, the probe can detect changes in plasma and the magnetic field.

“Right now we’re trying to figure out how far out are the influences of the sun felt,” she says.

The sun continuously spits out charged particles in a stream of solar wind that extends into space. That wind pushes back against the gas and other interstellar stuff surrounding our solar system, sculpting a bubble in space known as the heliosphere. “There will be some part farther out, some distance away [where the] interstellar medium has no idea that the heliosphere is even there,” she says. Rankin adds that she thinks Voyager 1 is right on the edge of this “undisturbed, pristine interstellar medium.”

It is something of a marvel that the almost 50-year-old Voyager 1 continues to supply astronomers with data. To send information to Earth, the probe uses a 23-watt radio transmitter (about the output of a small refrigerator lightbulb). Only antennas as sensitive as the 70-meter-wide dishes in the NASA Deep Space Network can detect Voyager 1’s super-faint signal. Without them, the space probe would have gone incommunicado years ago.

When Voyager 1 launched in September 1977, the nuclear-powered spacecraft had 10 operational scientific instruments. It discovered new moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn on its way out of our solar system; its observations of Jupiter’s moon Europa hinted at a liquid ocean under an icy crust. When the probe traveled beyond our solar system’s planets, NASA’s Voyager team shut down unnecessary equipment to conserve power. Now only two of its instruments are active. Ongoing management continues to preserve as much juice as possible from the spacecraft’s dwindling plutonium supply. The team was also forced to turn off the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment in April. In September, NASA swapped out three systems for lower-power alternatives on the Voyager 1, about six weeks after the same strategy worked on its twin Voyager 2 probe.

“It’s fun to see what sort of innovation people come up with to keep the spacecraft going,” Rankin says. “There’s only so much you can turn off.”

Voyagers 1 and 2 have been operating without several instrument heaters for years. If shutting those off hadn’t worked, Rankin says “the mission would have ended a decade ago.”

Still, its operational margins are thin. In late October, NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1; that issue has appeared to resolve itself and may have been related to a group of thrusters going offline.

“This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in a news release. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.” (JPL representatives did not respond to Popular Science’s requests for comment.)

All spacecraft missions must come to an end, no matter how plucky the probe or innovative its engineering team. NASA estimates that the Deep Space Network will lose contact with Voyager 1 around 2036, long before it travels to its two-light-day milestone. The probe may also freeze, unable to point properly back at Earth. Or its power systems will finally go kaput.

“We know that’s coming at some point. It’s probably not 20 years from now,” Rankin says. “It’s probably not 10 years from now.”

And then Voyager 1 will go forever radio silent as it cruises onward through the heavens.

#4628. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4627. Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.

Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of new car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

#4626. Rethinking Relationships Through the Lens of Asexuality

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

This post was co-written with Paula Bange and Laura Botzet, Ph.D.

The belief that sexuality is a universal and essential part of the human experience is deeply ingrained in our society. In pop culture, this assumption is especially visible. Reality TV shows like Too Hot To Handle are entirely built around the premise that people cannot resist sexual temptation. At the same time, these shows reflect the common idea that sexual attraction is closely tied to the beginning of romantic relationships. Accordingly, much of relationship science has been anchored in the idea that sexual attraction is a key mechanism guiding partner choice with the ultimate goal of having and raising children (1).

Asexuality, the lack of (or limited presence of) sexual attraction, challenges this long-held assumption. Looking at relationships through the lens of asexuality raises important questions: What do we really need for intimacy and connection? And does a fulfilling life necessarily require sexual attraction or a romantic partner?

If sexual attraction were a necessary condition for romantic love and relationships, asexual people must not want relationships. Right? This couldn’t be further from the truth. Research clearly shows that many asexual people seek emotionally intimate, close relationships but prefer not to engage in sexual intimacy (1, 2, 3, 4).

This highlights that romantic and sexual attraction don’t always go hand in hand. The split attraction model (5) distinguishes between different types of attraction, particularly sexual and romantic attraction, which do not always align. While many people experience both together, asexual people may experience romantic attraction without sexual desire. In other words, they might not desire sexual intercourse, but they fall in love, seek companionship, and build committed relationships.

At the same time, asexual people are less likely to be in romantic relationships (6) compared to allosexual people (individuals who experience sexual attraction). In addition, in our own work, we found that asexual women are more interested in being single in the future compared to heterosexual women (2). Given that decades of research have shown that being in a romantic relationship, especially a satisfying one, is linked to greater happiness, better health, and reduced loneliness (7), this seems like bad news.

Contradicting this assumption, being in a romantic relationship does not seem to protect against loneliness for asexual people in the same way it does for heterosexual, bisexual, and homosexual people (6). Even when asexual people are in a good relationship, it doesn’t reduce their loneliness as much as it does for other groups. Yet, being in a bad relationship doesn’t increase their loneliness as much either. In short, asexual people seem to be less affected—positively or negatively—by relationship quality compared to others. Dovetailing with these results, asexual singles are most satisfied with being single compared to other sexual orientations (8).

Together, these findings challenge the common belief that everyone wants and benefits from a romantic relationship. For asexual people, there may be even more good reasons to stay single. While some asexual people may prefer being single because they anticipate difficulties in finding a partner and maintaining a relationship that fits their needs, other asexual people do not experience romantic attraction and may not want any romantic relationship at all. Yet other forms of connection, such as friendships, may offer an important source of intimacy.

Indeed, emerging research shows that asexual people are more interested in, for example, alternative committed relationships than heterosexual people (2, 3, 4). These could be close friendships but may also take the form of emotionally close, committed, yet platonic partnerships. These so-called queer platonic partnerships are often described as deeply meaningful bonds that go beyond conventional friendship, while not necessarily involving romantic or sexual attraction (4). For asexual people in particular, queer platonic relationships may offer a way to experience closeness and commitment without the expectations tied to romance and sex.

Overall, asexual people seem to prefer constructing their ideal relationships outside of “traditional” scripts, yet more closely around their identity and needs. For example, asexual people may often date someone who experiences sexual attraction and wants to engage in sexual activities (3, 4). The couple will have to negotiate ways to meet both partners’ needs. Sometimes this may lead to consensually opening up relationships so that sexual needs can be met outside the relationship (2, 3). At the same time, research suggests that asexual people are less interested in becoming parents than allosexual people, indicating that having children may be less central for them or perceived as less normative (2). This further challenges key assumptions of research on partner selection that typically see reproduction as the ultimate goal.

Together, these findings highlight that asexual people are open to a variety of relationship structures and life paths.

Human experiences are diverse and so are asexual experiences. Differences in romantic and sexual attraction are just one piece of a much more complex picture of how people form relationships and define intimacy. Asexuality includes many different identities. For example, some asexual people do experience sexual attraction but only after they have formed an emotional bond with another person (demisexual), and others fall somewhere in between asexual and allosexual (graysexual) (9). All these nuances of (a)sexual experiences likely play a role in shaping what kind of relationship we are searching for.

Looking through the lens of asexuality reveals that there are different pathways to emotional connection and well-being. Relationships do not need to include sexual intimacy, not even romantic feelings, and can take on a multitude of forms. What asexuality teaches us is to rethink what intimacy and partnerships can look like and to recognize that a fulfilling life may not necessarily include a (romantic) partner altogether.

(1) Scheller, M., de Sousa, A. A., Brotto, L. A., & Little, A. C. (2023). The role of sexual and romantic attraction in human mate preferences. The Journal of Sex Research, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1080/00224499.2023.2176811

(2) Bange, P. C., Botzet, L. J., Shea, A. A., Vitzthum, V. J., & Gerlach, T. M. (2026). What do asexual women want? A propensity score matching study of preferred relationship options and ideal partner preferences. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 55(1), 345–368. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-025-03365-2

(3) Dawson, M., McDonnell, L., & Scott, S. (2016). Negotiating the boundaries of intimacy: The personal lives of asexual people. The Sociological Review, 64(2), 349–365. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-954x.12362

(4) Higginbottom, B. (2024). The nuances of intimacy: Asexual perspectives and experiences with dating and relationships. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 53(5), 1899–1914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-024-02846-0

(5) Winer, C. (2025). Splitting attraction: Differentiating romantic and sexual orientations among asexual individuals. Social Currents, 12(3), 215–230. https://doi.org/10.1177/23294965241305170

(6) Zoppolat, G., Barreto, M., Qualter, P., Crosbie, J., & Doyle, D. M. (2026). Does romantic involvement benefit everyone? Testing a foundational tenet in relationship science through the case of asexuality. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 19485506261437286. https://doi.org/10.1177/19485506261437286

(7) Kansky, J. (2018). What's love got to do with it? Romantic relationships and well-being. In E. Diener, S. Oishi, & L. Tay (Eds.), Handbook of well-being. DEF Publishers.

(8) Febe Canaletti, E., D. Krämer, M., Stern, J., A. Pepping, C., Park, Y., & MacDonald, G. (2026). The Solo Rainbow: A Descriptive Examination of Single People’s Well-Being Across Sexual Identities. Journal of Happiness Studies, 27(8), 151. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10902-026-01138-9

(9) Copulsky, D., & Hammack, P. L. (2023). Asexuality, graysexuality, and demisexuality: Distinctions in desire, behavior, and identity. The Journal of Sex Research, 60(2), 221–230. https://doi.org/10.1080/00224499.2021.2012113

#4625. Fake rocks boost survival for venomous Australian snakes

Published Nov 9, 2026 11:48 AM EST

Australia’s broad-headed snake (Hoplocephalus bungaroides) is as unique as it is threatened. However, ecologists at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) have good news about this reptile. According to researchers, four of six captive-bred juveniles recently released into the Australian bush have survived their initial, most dangerous months outdoors. The team’s first-of-its-kind program may provide a promising path forward for the species—and a set of bespoke, artificial rocks may be the key.

“Reintroducing any threatened species is challenging, especially when they’re captive bred,” explained University of Technology Sydney (UTS) wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb. “When the juvenile snakes are released, they risk getting eaten by either native predators, like kookaburras and brown snakes, or invasive predators such as cats or foxes.”

The broad-headed snake’s current predicament is the result of multiple issues. The distinct, yellow-banded serpent is slow to mature, and only begins reproducing around five years old. When it does, the nearly three-foot-long snake is one of the only venomous species known to give birth to live offspring. Although adults can live as long as 23 years in their native Sydney Basin, females only mate every two or three years. This leaves the broad-headed snake extremely susceptible to climate change, human impacts, and invasive predators. Any disruptions to the reproductive cycle can destabilize Australia’s population for generations—and the species has experienced plenty of disruptions over the last few decades.

“The broad-headed snake fascinated me because it used to be very common in the Sydney region, but even in the 1990’s it was quite rare,” said Webb. “Why was this species in trouble when other snake species were doing okay?”

Webb noted that Australia’s increasingly frequent droughts and wildfires, coupled with habitat destruction, have made the broad-headed snake one the continent’s most threatened species. The intentional removal of bush-rocks for landscaping projects is also rough on the animals.Juveniles are particularly hard hit, as they rely on the bush-rocks for shelter and a steady diet of other reptiles like skinks and geckos.

“You can still buy rocks and boulders taken from the bush at your local landscape supplier, which is something I find really frustrating,” said Webb, adding that a single attractive boulder can sell for as much as $450. “That’s a pretty strong incentive for people.”

In collaboration with the conservation organization Aussie Ark and Indigenous representatives of the Traditional Owners of the Shoalhaven region, Webb’s team have bred eight broad-headed snakes in captivity since 2024. Biologists kept one pair of snakes for their genetics, then released the other six at restoration sites in May. However, the juveniles weren’t left stranded in the bush. Researchers placed them beneath custom artificial rocks designed with ideal crevice measurements to mirror natural geologic formations’ thermal properties. Webb said the rocks were “critical” to the snakes’ survival odds.

“Broad-headed snakes are nocturnal so they shelter under these rocks during the day and rely on them for warmth, protection and to attract prey,” he explained.

Biologists hope to expand the program elsewhere in Australia, and breed even more broad-headed snakes for release. Although it’s a slow process, their early successes indicate a potentially ecosystem-altering solution for the reptiles.

“We now have a unique, multi-faceted, holistic program that’s a model for threatened species conservation Australia-wide, and I couldn’t be prouder of our team and our partners,” added Aussie Ark founder Tim Faulkner.

#4624. Bald eagle Shadow defends Kaydee and his nest from intruder

Published Nov 9, 2026 12:54 PM EST

Word to the wise: don’t mess with Shadow’s nest. For the first time in two weeks, the internet-famous bald eagle’s (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) vocals were heard on the camera that captures a 24/7 livestream of his nest in Southern California. Shadow’s potentially new partner Kaydee was also heard nearby and she landed on the nest.

However, just after landing, Kaydee was on high alert because another eagle was eyeing the nest from above. Shadow quickly responded with loud vocals, and came swooping past the nest. While the intruding eagle briefly followed Shadow away, it made a turn back towards the nest. Kaydee made more calls to Shadow and quickly flew out of the nest, as the intruder tried to land on the branches above her. Shadow returned to the nest, and put himself between Kaydee and the intruder above, and all three birds flew away. Eventually, Shadow perched on a nearby tree and was heard giving a warning call in a loud voice while standing watch. The scene that appeared straight out of a movie was another exciting moment for the eagles of Big Bear Valley.

“The brief encounter last night definitely showed Shadow and Kaydee defending the nest, protecting it and each other,” writes Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the livestream. “What a delight to see them as they have truly been missed these past two weeks!”

According to FOBBV, Shadow is ALSO an “experienced master builder and knows exactly when it’s time to begin tidying up the nest, moving stick furniture or placing new guardrails or a baby gate.”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting officially begins in September, and lasts over six months, depending on when the the chicks fledge. Eggs are typically laid in January.  Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Big Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.
